claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC RHEA.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has high density and insufficient room-temperature ductility.
Adding a minor amount of V or Cr to Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will induce a C15 Laves phase.
Annealing at 900 °C will induce Laves-phase precipitation or phase separation in the modified alloy.
The induced secondary phase will be a C15 AB2 Laves phase.
The precipitated phase will be Hf2Mo or a chemically similar intermetallic.
The C15 phase will form a reticulated network at grain boundaries and triple junctions in the BCC matrix.
The Laves-phase network will act as a physical barrier that deflects, branches, or bridges cracks and increases crack-path tortuosity.
The BCC matrix will retain ductility after formation of the Laves-phase network.
Microstructural heterogeneity can promote strength-ductility synergy in HEAs, including refractory BCC systems.
The intervention will significantly increase both yield strength and room-temperature compressive ductility relative to the baseline alloy.
The intervention will cause less than a 2% density increase.
The baseline alloy's low room-temperature ductility is caused by high lattice friction and the absence of crack-deflection mechanisms.
Keeping the Laves-phase volume fraction below approximately 15-20% will avoid a percolation threshold for brittleness.
A continuous Laves-phase network, rather than isolated particles, is required for the proposed mechanical-property improvement.
Laves-phase formation is thermodynamically favorable in the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr system upon annealing.
Thin-film evidence suggests that Laves-phase formation increases hardness.

contradictions.description: The operating regime is uniaxial compression, but the proposed ductility outcome and measurement are stated as uniform elongation. Uniform elongation is ordinarily a tensile metric and is not directly obtained from a compression stress-strain curve.
